articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks to Rally on US Tech Surge, Oil Slump: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:

"Markets bottom on bad news," is one of those smart-sounding rules of thumb that proves true just often enough to remain a Wall Street cliché in good standing.
Did the brutal weeks-long punishment of AI stocks culminate last week and reverse higher Monday after a pileup of adverse headlines? In the past week, American voters resoundingly opposed data-center construction across much of the country and Anthropic lowered its target IPO valuation just before a sex-and-espionage scandal struck the one-man embodiment of the entire AI economy, Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
The story of a market taking a cue from a crescendo of bad news after a nasty setback to stage a resounding bounce holds together well enough for now, after Monday's 3.4% jump in the Nasdaq-100 and 7% rip in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), even as Nvidia shed 4.3%.
Based purely on the tactical evidence, the tech-hardware complex came into the week pretty well washed out and primed to bounce. Numerous trading desks reported historically rare intensity of net selling in the group by institutions into last Thursday's risk purge. The Nasdaq-100 was as oversold on several metrics as it had been at the March 30 Iran-selloff low. The CBOE S&P 500 Volatility Index has put in a nice spike of the sort usually associated with a passing storm, shooting up to 28 and then receding below 20.
The recent dump in the Nasdaq and uptick in risk aversion, "had many elements of capitulation," says Laurent Laskowski, options strategist at Baird Strategas: "record options activity, a sharp spike in volatility, skew and correlations, an inverted VIX curve, and forced liquidations…The setup, therefore, is one where the market is seeing the [downside] left tail narrowing while the [upside] right tail is fattening."
Several technical-analysis gurus (including Macro Risk Advisors' John Kolovos, whose work is cited below) argue the market hasn't quite served up a "fat pitch" to buy the pullback aggressively. Maybe so. But FanGraphs calculates that in Major League Baseball only about 7% of all pitches are in the very center of the strike zone. While those fat pitches result in some 23% of all home runs hit, the other three-quarters of balls that fly over the wall come with less-perfect setups around the edges of the zone.
I wouldn't argue too strenuously against this tech-centered rally carrying on for a bit, for these reasons as well as the fact that valuations have become far less demanding. Last week, I noted Big Tech had not to that point responded to moderately stressed conditions but was getting closer, and "the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market." Monday's blip higher could be a start, with plenty still to prove.
But this AI-driven part of the market has lately shown itself less worthy of investor trust, leaving enough hints of structural damage to the bull case that faith can't be restored right away.
In a late-June column , I asked, "Was May 14 a consequential moment for this market, at least tactically?" That date, nearly six months ago, was when the S&P 500 spurted higher to reach the 7500 level for the first time; the index has never reached escape velocity since and in fact crossed above 7500 again just yesterday.
May 14 was when highly touted AI-chip upstart Cerebras came public and its shares more than doubled to a high of $386, as President Trump and China's leader were reported to have made progress on ending the Iran war. Since then, Cerebras has collapsed to $97, the semiconductor group is off 17% and the Iran conflict continues.
A month later the SpaceX IPO was another apparent culmination of New Era tech enthusiasm; it might not have been an important peak in AI excitement, but if it were the market action since would possibly resemble what we've seen since.
Perhaps a half-year reckoning period during which the market has refused to pay up for 30% annual earnings growth for two straight quarters is enough to build a new base constructed on more modest expectations. I've been focused on late-cycle tremors unsettling markets in the form of peak earnings growth, peak capex, peak index concentration, a tighter Federal Reserve and credit flareups. This all explains the market's multi-month stall, and they remain.
But it's important to remain open to the chance that these could end up amounting to mere mid-cycle turbulence, as Morgan Stanley chief investment officer Mike Wilson has been arguing .
First, though, the tape will need to show more progress than a nice, broad single-day comeback. Another rule of thumb holds that a rebound rally needs at least to carry above the 20-day moving average to prove that it's not merely a reflexive dead-cat bounce. This would require a 1.3% gain from Monday's close for the S&P 500, 3.7% for the Nasdaq-100 and 9% for the SOX.
Without pretending any clear sense of what the various Nvidia investigations will mean for its China sales, leadership or long-term earnings power, we can say for sure that the scandal arrived at a fairly opportune time for the market.
Valuations have been pounded to multi-year lows on persistent worry that current profits are unsustainable and the group remains vulnerable to any slowdown in data-center builds. This allowed, for a day, every other semiconductor stock to whistle higher as Nvidia lost some $200 billion in market cap on a blistering $80 billion in dollar-volume traded in the stock.
The S&P 500 as a whole, of course, has grown optically cheaper, too, with semis bolstering the projected earnings and investors declining to give the group credit for their sustainability.
The issue remains that less of those earnings are set to manifest as free cash flow as the hyperscalers spend manically. As this chart comparing the valuation gauges shows, the market looks a good deal less cheap on free cash flow than earnings.
A proper bull case for the market from here might be that the likes of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft will resume harvesting free cash flow, on which investors might place a higher multiple than they're willing to bestow on those hot but hard-to-trust chip makers. Not yet a provable argument.
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "While sentiment is dire, our concern is that technology is in a 'bad oversold' condition, where seductive bounces fail to produce lasting lows. Instead, the broader equity market may need to follow technology lower, with a more widespread capitulation ultimately needed to wash out weak hands and establish a durable bottom."

Huge privately financed infrastructure buildout, destabilizing new habits of interaction with technology and constant calls for government regulation in exchange for near-monopoly power. The book cites an AT&T ad from 1909 calling telephones "tools of 'civilization . . . one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence.'"

The main reasons are sobering though, with most gains coming from data-center construction and wealth creation for those who own AI-dependent stocks. Cold comfort for information-economy job seekers.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic seeks $1.4 trillion valuation in highly anticipated IPO amid AI boom
articles.title_zh: Anthropic seeks $1.4 trillion valuation in highly anticipated IPO amid AI boom
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at $1.3 trillion (Â£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and plans to raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
This would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some analysts had predicted weeks ago.
It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.
Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.
Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could be a problem for the economy
articles.content_orig:
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., said on a Tuesday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.
And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.
"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.
"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."
Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday.
The New York Times reported that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies have identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia opened an investigation into its CEO on Sunday. The two Huangs are not related.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"
Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.

articles.title_orig: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: Iran rejects French claims it was behind supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
Shelves were left bare by the cyber-attacks
Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as "baseless and hostile".
On Monday, the French authorities blamed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for the string of hacks, which foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said were "unprecedented" in terms of their scale and "level of aggression".
He added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions.
The French cyber-attacks, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food, were followed by a similar hacks against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
On Monday, some Iranian media outlets denied the French accusations, but there had been no official comment until Tuesday's statement from Iran's foreign ministry.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title_orig: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.title_zh: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.content_orig:
Solange Alexandre twice turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur before relenting in 2024
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104.  Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.
After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of RuillÃ©-sur-Loir.
With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.
"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.
Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France,  Solange Alexandre, nÃ©e Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.
"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917.   The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.
In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany.  She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.
"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.
Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's â a Tunisian-born French army veteran called SaÃ¯d Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.
Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.
"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.
In 1943 she met her first husband Guy DÃ©liot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.
The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.
Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy.  There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.
"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.
After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).
Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.
Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur , saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.
Finally in 2024 she relented.
On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour.  I am very proud â even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

articles.title_orig: U.S., Russia and Ukraine begin talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: U.S., Russia and Ukraine begin talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The United States, Ukraine and Russia have started talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday aimed at ending the war in Ukraine that began in 2022 when Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of his country's neighbor .
The two-day session is the first such meeting since February and will focus on security guarantees, a long-running demand from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner said in a post on X that he and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff were "working hard to find a negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."
Kushner indicated these talks are just an initial step but could "build momentum" toward future negotiations. He also suggested a future agreement would involve a security arrangement involving European countries and Russia.
But on Tuesday both Russia and Ukraine seemed to pour cold water on the initiative.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia rejects European demands for a ceasefire in Ukraine, asserting that Brussels was just trying to "buy time" for Kyiv.
"We will not agree to this," he said.
He added that Moscow did not want to prevent the U.S. from engaging with Europe on the Ukraine war, but it does not consider that to be the best approach.
Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.
Zelenskyy posted on Telegram , meanwhile, that the U.S. had asked if Kyiv would "'trade the Donbas for security," but that the U.S. said that did not mean Ukraine joining NATO, "'but something similar.'"
"No one believes that Putin will stop if we give up the Donbas," he added. "He might pause — but then he will return in a year, two years, or five years. And who will be to blame then?"
Putin has previously said he wanted Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, the four regions Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demanded that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Zelenskyy rejected Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejected any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
The U.S., Russia and Ukraine have held three other rounds of trilateral talks this year, in January and February, but diplomatic efforts largely stalled after Mr. Trump launched a war on Iran. Since then, Witkoff and Kushner have held various separate meetings with Putin and Zelenskyy.
In October, first lady Melania Trump's office said she had secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons. It lasted from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1.

articles.title_orig: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
articles.title_zh: How GM is trying to talk used car shoppers into buying new vehicles
articles.content_orig:
Affordability challenges are pushing some buyers out of the new vehicle market. Many are choosing used cars instead.
In turn, automakers are looking for ways to compete with many of the online retailers grabbing market share in the used car market and trying to bring some of those customers back into a new vehicle.
New vehicle sales tend to be more profitable for automakers, but reselling trade-ins as used vehicles is highly profitable for dealers. Used car prices are relatively strong, but newer online retailers such as Carvana and CarMax have made the market more competitive for dealers and other incumbent used car sellers.
"The internet and technology and apps on our phone have changed every aspect of retail, and probably one of the slowest areas of retail to have adopted to online and digital shopping has been the auto industry," said Ivan Feinseth, partner, chief investment officer and director of research at Tigress Financial Partners.
General Motors is a key example of automakers' attempts to address this shifting market. The automaker has revamped its certified used vehicle program, which now operates under the CarBravo name. It's essentially an online portal through which Chevrolet, Buick and GMC dealers can list their certified used vehicles and make them available to customers all over the U.S.
About 1,615 of GM's 3,700 dealers are enrolled in the program, according to the company. The only GM brand not involved is Cadillac, which maintains its own program.
"Certified" used or "preowned" vehicles are used cars that have undergone a thorough inspection and reconditioning. They typically come with guarantees and warranties from the manufacturer.
Many automakers have certified used programs for their own cars. But GM, as part of its revamp, is using CarBravo to certify vehicles made by other automakers. A lot of those cars arrive at dealerships as trade-ins, and often dealers will sell them to wholesale auctions, said John Fitzpatrick, senior manager of the CarBravo program.
"Wholesaling doesn't bring nearly the revenue that selling it to a new customer does," he said.
GM has said it is planning to net about 250,000 sales in its CarBravo program in 2026. Fitzpatrick said he doesn't expect that even half of those will end up being new car sales.
But through CarBravo, the customer gets access to GM's dealership network for service, something Fitzpatrick says is a key differentiator between its program and growing online sellers. CarBravo vehicles come with various warranties, depending on the age and mileage on the car.
GM said the program is driving more traffic into local dealerships, where purchases are typically finalized. That creates an opportunity to convert a used car shopper into a new car buyer. So far, the automaker said about 38% of the shoppers initially looking for used cars end up buying new.
A customer who wants to buy a full-size truck can look on the website and compare used Chevrolet Silverados alongside used Ford F-150s and Ram 1500s, for example. The buyer might settle on a used truck from any of those brands, but a conversation with a dealer can push them in a different direction.
"The customer picks up the phone, but in the back of their mind, they maybe always have been a traditional, more new car customer," Fitzpatrick said.
"You've shown the customer, you're going to pay $500 [per month] for this used F-150, but you may pay $510 or $515 for this new Chevy," he said. "And now all of a sudden the customer says, yeah, maybe I can do that because I'd rather have that new vehicle than the used truck."
While the average transaction price of a new vehicle is about $50,000, the average 3-year-old used car costs about $30,000 as of September, according to Cox Automotive.
However, industry analysts say customers base their purchasing decisions on the cost of the monthly payment more than on the sticker price of the car.
New cars often come with longer-term loan options than used ones, Feinseth said, which can result in lower monthly payments.
"On a 1- or 2-year-old car, you may be only stuck with a 3- or 4-year loan," he said. "On a new car, you can get a 5-year, 6-year loan."
The share of new car loans lasting 84 months hit a new record in the third quarter, at more than 1 in 4 loans, according to Edmunds.
Meanwhile, used car prices in some affordable segments have risen, according to Cox Automotive, and about three quarters of consumers express some interest in certified cars.
But the key is building the relationship with the customer, he said. About 50% of the buyers GM has gained through the program appear to be new to the brand, meaning there is no record of them in any of the automaker's customer databases. About 70% had never visited the dealership they ended up purchasing from.
"The goal is really to get that customer engaged with the store, give them the option of building a relationship with the dealer," he said. "The dealer can really help the customer figure out what works for their budget."
It's a boon for dealers too: Customers buying warranty-backed used cars often return to the dealership for service visits — which often account for about half of a dealership's profits. GM can also sell subscriptions to connected vehicle services, such as its OnStar, which provides safety, security and navigation services.
"That is a big part of General Motors' business going forward, is to sell the software and subscription services like OnStar and eventually to the cars that are enabled with Super Cruise," GM's advanced driver-assistance system, Feinseth said.
GM isn't the only automaker trying to use its certified preowned vehicle program to lure buyers.
Detroit rival Ford Motor also certifies vehicles made by other manufacturers through its Ford Blue Advantage program. It is on track to do 450,000 total sales in 2026, more than GM's 250,000 target. It didn't specify how many of those buyers end up purchasing new vehicles.
Toyota told CNBC in an email that about 40% of its used car shoppers end up buying new instead.
Honda didn't give specifics about its program. But Lance Woelfer, American Honda's vice president of automobile sales, said conversions happen "probably every day at dealerships throughout the country."
"But it also is more about that first interaction with the consumer," Woelfer said. "And there are people in any market that prefer to buy a used vehicle, but appreciate the confidence that a [certified preowned designation] can give them."
Woelfer said those customers come back to get their vehicles serviced at a rate about 18% higher than someone who buys a non-certified used car. They also return to purchase a new car at a rate about 7% to 8% higher in the future, he said.
"It's about that first relationship that allows us to then have that customer loyalty for life," he added. "And that's where our focus is. We've been doing it a long time, and we've seen a lot of benefits from the certified business."

The final cut of Blacktalon launches on Warhammer TV this week! It’s more than three and a half hours of action-packed animation following Sigmar’s legendary hunter.
And before that, there’s the debut of Khazalite Holds on Battle Report and exclusive interviews with author Robert Rath and Golden Demon legend Albert Moreto Font. Let’s dig in…
The forces of the Khazalite Holds make their Battle Report debut in a bitter clash against their fallen kin – the Helsmiths of Hashut. Can guest player Jay, from the Warhammer Studio, overcome the followers of the Bullfather in an epic 2,000 point bout?
Since this is the first time that the Khazalite Holds have done battle on Warhammer TV, we thought it might be good to share Jay’s army list to give some ideas of how to blend together Grimmdron (or Fyreslayers as you might still know them) and Kromdron.
Battle Formation: Hearthsworn Defenders Heroic Trait: Innate Resonance Artefact of Power: Deep-earth Runic Weapon Spell Lore: Reverberations of the Runes Manifestation Lore: Aetherwrought Machineries Runefather on Magmadroth Runeson on Magmadroth 5 Auric Hearthguard 9 Vulkyn Flameseekers Hjulda Drakkblud Thrynn 10 Clanshields 10 Clanshields Runewright Oathkeeper Cannon Stonebreaker Mortar 3 Gholems of Gazul
Jay went with the Hearthsworn Defenders battle formation, giving his force access to the Lock Shields! ability, making them particularly durable against enemy shooting when defending their home territory or a crucial objective.
Dug in and resolute, little can pierce the well-made defences of these duardin.
Effect: Subtract 1 from hit rolls for shooting attacks that target friendly KHAZALITE HOLDS units while they are wholly within friendly territory or while every model in the unit is contesting an objective you control.
We sat down with Battle Report host Si (who commanded the Helsmiths of Hashut) to learn what it was like to face the newest faction in Warhammer Age of Sigmar.
Warhammer Community: What were your first impressions of fighting against the Khazalite Holds?
Si: Don’t expect to outshoot them! Even without any Clangunners, Jay’s artillery – he had an Oathkeeper Cannon and a Stonebreaker Mortar – was a constant menace to my army, while the accuracy of my own ranged units was hampered by his Locked Shields. What was worse, after winning priority in the first battle round, Jay moved aggressively to secure the forward objectives and thereby expand the battle formation’s area of effect beyond his territory. I mean, a Deathshrieker Rocket Battery can hit with truly devastating force, but when it’s reduced to hitting on a 5+, it’s far less reliable.
WarCom: In many ways the Helsmiths of Hashut are a dark mirror of the Khazalite Holds – how do they compare as armies?
Si: Aside from the more obvious nuances that their respective faction rules offer, I would say that the key differences lie in speed in the case of the Helsmiths versus the even heavier armour of the Kromdron units in particular. Okay, so Helmsmiths are far from the fastest faction, but their access to hard-hitting cavalry units in the form of Anointed Sentinels and Bull Centaurs gives them an edge over their bipedal cousins, while their Infernal Taurus-riding Daemonsmiths can Fly, unlike the Khazalites on War Thrones or Magmadroths. Of course, the Khazalites make up for this relative shortfall* with an overwhelming number of 3+ Save characteristics as well as multiple ways to mitigate the effectiveness of incoming attacks.
WarCom: Are there any particular Khazalite Holds combinations that opponents need to keep an eye out for?
Si: At first glance, it would be easy to overlook the potential of Clanshields . However, pair them up with a Thrynn, or better still, Hjulda Drakkblud, and they can become a real force to be reckoned with. Under the right circumstances, you can improve four of the five characteristics of their Kromdron Weapons without the use of any command abilities, all the while reducing the Rend of incoming attacks and ignoring the first damage point they suffer in each phase. Underestimate them at your peril!
WarCom: Do you have any tips for players wanting to defeat the Khazalites?
Si: Well, as I mentioned earlier, they’re tough opponents to outshoot, so you really need to take the fight to them if you want to avoid being shot to pieces. That being said, breaking through the Khazalite lines to counter their artillery and powerful ranged units is easier said than done. This is where abilities that enable you to instantly relocate across the battlefield or otherwise break through their lines can come in clutch. Judicious use of pile-ins or a well-timed Power Through, for example, may help you to bog down a key ranged unit before they can shoot you in the following turn.**
WarCom: Finally, do you have a favourite unit from the new battletome?
Si: Hmm… It would be easy to say High Kyng Valankrom, as he’s not only a magnificent model (or should that be diorama?), but he’s a real force multiplier, and rock-solid in a fight. That being said, I think I’d actually have to say the humble Clanshields. I don’t think I would leave the hold without two reinforced units of 20 to form the backbone of my Khazalite throng.
Thanks, Si! Tune in to see if the infernal sorcery of Daemonsmith Urak Taar is enough to hold back the tide of vengeance that seeks to smash his forces, and don’t forget that the new Khazalite Holds miniatures are available to pre-order now .
Robert Rath, author of fan-favourite novel The Infinite and the Divine is the guest on Scribes and Scriveners , talking about his latest novel, The Wicked and the Warped . The sequel sees Orikan the Diviner and Trazyn the Infinite thrown into an unlikely alliance to uncover the secrets of a rediscovered world from ancient Necron history.
Presenter Alex talks to Robert about his latest novel and what exactly this means for Orikan and Trazyn’s relationship – can they finally set aside their differences or are they doomed to an eternity of petty bickering?
This week on Painting Desk , presenter Ed is joined by multiple Slayer Sword winner Albert Moreto Font . Albert talks about his painting journey, how he made his start in Warhammer, and how he has managed to stay passionate and motivated throughout years of competitions. He also gives a unique insight into the world of competition painting, the importance of the wider community, and even dispels a few myths around Golden Demon .

articles.title_orig: IDF prepares for surprise Iranian attack as US pursues deal with Tehran
articles.title_zh: IDF prepares for surprise Iranian attack as US pursues deal with Tehran
articles.content_orig:
The IDF is preparing for two major escalation scenarios involving Iran as the United States, steered by US Vice President JD Vance, continues diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement with Tehran and preventing a broader regional conflict.
The talks are focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restoring international nuclear inspections in exchange for partially lifting the US blockade on Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets. Israeli defense officials remain on high alert as diplomatic efforts continue alongside limited US military strikes.
The first scenario the IDF has prepared for involves the United States launching an extensive and particularly aggressive military offensive against Iran, targeting national infrastructure and military facilities in an effort to shorten the conflict and bring it to an end.
The second scenario involves Iran attempting a surprise attack against American interests and military bases across the Middle East, including IDF bases hosting US military personnel and aircraft.
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir and senior General Staff officers have held discussions and situational assessments in recent days to review and validate operational plans.
As a result of these discussions, Israel Air Force Commander Maj.-Gen. Omer Tishler and Operations Directorate head Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen did not attend the IDF Commanders' Championship.
The assessments cover a wide range of scenarios and potential responses, aimed at ensuring operational readiness in the event of a surprise Iranian attack.
The military is also preparing for the possibility that Israel's adversaries in its immediate and wider regional surroundings could become involved in an escalation, whether through a coordinated operation, misunderstanding, or miscalculation.
Meanwhile, Israeli defense officials assess that US President Donald Trump would prefer to avoid a military confrontation and resolve tensions through a diplomatic agreement.
However, Israeli security assessments suggest that the Iranian leadership views Washington's preference for diplomacy as a sign of weakness.
According to these assessments, Tehran views the results of the US midterm elections , held on Tuesday, November 3, as a form of political "revenge" against the White House.
Israeli officials also believe Iran is unlikely to rush into signing an agreement and will instead maintain a hard-line negotiating position while attempting to prolong the talks.
In recent days, US forces have carried out limited strikes against Iranian military assets in the south of the country and around the Strait of Hormuz, including operations targeting air defense systems and missile launchers on Qeshm Island.
Additional reported operations have targeted Iranian military positions on Larak Island, while Iranian forces have retaliated against American military assets and vessels in the region. The timing and full extent of all the reported strikes have not been independently confirmed.
The military developments have unfolded alongside ongoing diplomatic contacts, highlighting the risk that limited exchanges could escalate despite efforts to reach an agreement.
Separately, Israeli defense officials addressed discussions held on November 1, two days before the US midterm elections, during which senior security officials reviewed potential scenarios and responses involving Iran.
Among the options raised was the possibility of a preemptive Israeli offensive against Iran, reportedly supported by the Mossad chief.
However, security officials said they considered the proposal and then dropped it, rejecting suggestions that the discussions involved unusually heated disagreements.
"The option was raised and then dropped just as quickly," security officials said. "The discussion was professional and respectful. There were disagreements on some issues, but no arguments that got out of proportion."
"The leaks from the discussion were politically motivated," the officials added.

articles.title_orig: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
articles.title_zh: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. They would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped up security.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.
Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to airbases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk.
It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain , RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike the Islamic Republic.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on this week’s movements and said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and remained under discussion by U.S. officials.
“We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News.
“U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement,” a U.S. European Command official said. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets,” the European Command official added.
A spokesperson for the U.K.’s Ministry of Defense said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.”
“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said.
It comes weeks after the U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials previously told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at that base, located in Gloucestershire.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. Other arrests followed and two men were charged under the National Security Act.
The incident, which attracted huge international attention, remains largely unexplained although British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the activity was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
Though Tehran has denied involvement in any plot against RAF Fairford, its powerful Revolutionary Guard warned in July that any base used to launch attacks against Iranian territory was a legitimate target.
Iran has vowed retaliation for any renewal of the American-Israeli war against it and has threatened to expand its response beyond the Middle East.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington had addressed concerns around reported threats from Tehran against American diplomats overseas by “moving people away from the threat.”
“Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas,” Rubio said. “And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.”
Citing new “momentum” in negotiations to end the war, President Donald Trump on Monday downplayed the prospect of new U.S. attacks.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said following a meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani.
Further U.S. attacks “won’t be necessary” at this point, but Washington remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, Trump told reporters at the White House.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Matthew Mulligan is a senior reporter for the NBC News Social Newsgathering team based in London.

articles.title_orig: Israel's new parliament to be sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.title_zh: Israel's new parliament to be sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.content_orig:
Israel's new parliament will be sworn in on Tuesday, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief was tasked with forming a government by the president, after he received the backing of 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset, compared to 46 for Netanyahu.
But Eisenkot faces an uphill struggle. His bloc of four parties won 48 seats in last month's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the MKs being sworn in did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
Netanyahu - Israel's longest-serving leader - reiterated in a video on Monday his call for the formation of a government of national unity, which he said he would lead as prime minister.
He said any Zionist party - those which support Israel as a Jewish state - including opposition parties, would be eligible. He warned against a government which relied on what he called "the Islamists", an apparent reference to Arab parties.
"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters," he said.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30%, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30%, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian drones struck the KINEF refinery in Russia's Leningrad region on Monday, causing major fires and damaging three oil processing units.
Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defences shot down 113 drones targeting the region, but debris from one struck the roof of a multi-storey building in Vsevolozhsk, killing a resident.
Three main processing units at the Kirishinefteorgsintez (KINEF) plant were damaged.
KINEF, the largest refinery in northwest Russia and second largest in the country behind the Omsk facility, is owned by the Surgutneftegaz group and processes roughly 18 million tonnes of crude oil a year, about 7% of Russia's total refining capacity.
The plant produces petrol, diesel, aviation kerosene, fuel oil, bitumen and petrochemical products, and supplies aviation fuel to St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport. Its design capacity is 20-21 million tonnes annually.
The refinery has been targeted multiple times by Ukrainian forces since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Surgutneftegaz was placed under EU, US and UK sanctions in 2025.
Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces shot down 430 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions and occupied Crimea overnight. Euronews could not independently verify these claims.
Rosneft announced on Monday it was capping petrol and diesel sales at its filling stations. The restrictions took effect in Karelia, Buryatia, Zabaykalsky Krai, and the Novosibirsk, Arkhangelsk and Penza regions, according to Russian media.
In cities, customers are limited to 30 litres of petrol per transaction; on motorways, the cap is 50 litres. In Krasnoyarsk Krai, separate limits apply: 30 litres of AI-95, 50 litres of AI-92 and 100 litres of diesel per customer.
Authorities in Leningrad region also recommended filling stations cap petrol sales at 30 litres and diesel at 50 litres per transaction.
Russian forces launched 317 Shahed drones since Monday evening, including 105 jet-powered variants and Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and decoy drones, Ukraine's air force said. Of these, 276 were shot down. Impacts were recorded in 31 locations and falling debris in nine more.
A drone strike on a food warehouse in Odesa on Monday morning killed three people and left one in serious condition.
Two people were killed and seven injured in strikes on Dnipropetrovsk region. Nine people, including children, were injured in attacks on Kharkiv region overnight on Tuesday.
Six people, including one child, were wounded in strikes on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding area.
Seven people were injured in a drone strike on Kremenchuk in Poltava region, among them a 16-year-old. A rehabilitation centre for children with disabilities was destroyed in the attack.
In Sumy, three power workers were injured on Monday morning when a Russian strike hit their vehicle.
Russian forces struck rescue teams in Kamyshivakha three times with drones as they cleared rubble from a Russian air strike on 2 November that killed 55 people. Up to 19 may still be trapped under the debris. Police have identified 30 of the dead.

In 2017, Apple celebrated the iPhone's 10th birthday with the iPhone X, the biggest redesign in the product's history. For the device's 20th anniversary, all the rumors indicate that the company is preparing another landmark redesign.
The commemorative "iPhone 20" model isn't expected until September 2027, but leaks have been piling up for months. According to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman, Apple is already deep into its development , and the picture forming across multiple reports is of an iPhone that looks like a single, uninterrupted slab of glass. With all that said, we're still ahead of a rumored fall 2027 launch, and Apple's plans shift constantly behind closed doors, plus features this ambitious have a habit of slipping a year or two. Under-display Face ID in particular has been "two years away" for about five years now.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Preloading Is Live. Here's How to Install the Game on PlayStation and Xbox
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Preloading Is Live. Here's How to Install the Game on PlayStation and Xbox
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
After over a decade of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is nearly here. While the game officially releases on November 19 , you can now preload it onto your PlayStation or Xbox. If you're new to this, that means you'll be able to install the full game on your console's drive ahead of its release. That way, when the game unlocks in your time zone, you'll be ready to go.
Since GTA 6 is a massive game—both in popularity and file size—we highly recommend preloading it, if you can. Here's how to start your install and how long it will take to download.
Grand Theft Auto 6 preload times vary by gaming platform. On Xbox, preloads for digital versions went live at 12 a.m. GMT on November 10 for Series X and Series S , which translates to 7 p.m. EST / 6 p.m. CST / 5 p.m. MST / 4 p.m. PT on Monday, November 9. For PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro owners, preloading started on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time.
If you ordered a physical copy of GTA 6, games will begin arriving at retailers and shipping to buyers on November 12. You can use the code in your box to preload your copy of the game.
The main reason we suggest preloading this single-player game is because of its massive file size. Rockstar Games announced that GTA 6 will be 212 GB once downloaded. That could take up a significant portion of your SSD on any console , but you'll need to be especially careful if you plan to play on the original Xbox Series S, which has just 512GB of internal storage.
If you've preordered Grand Theft Auto 6, you can preload the game by going to the PlayStation Store, navigating to your preordered copy of GTA 6, and selecting Preload or Download.
You can also set up your PlayStation 5 to automatically download the game file. Set this up by going to Game Library , selecting the pre-ordered game, and making sure Auto-Download is enabled. Make sure you leave your PS5 os PS5 Pro powered on or in Rest Mode for it to work.
If you've preordered GTA 6 on Xbox, you can begin downloading the game now by going to the Microsoft Store, searching for Grand Theft Auto 6, and selecting Install.
To enable pre-downloads, head to Profile & system > Settings > System > Updates and make sure Keep My Games & Apps Up to Date is enabled for automatic updates. Your Xbox must be powered on or in Sleep mode for this to work.
Is it actually worth preloading your game before the actual release date? For a game this popular that takes up 212GB on your console's storage, it's smart to get a head start so you're not stuck waiting on launch day. That said, exactly how long it will take to preload depends on a variety of factors, but there's a quick-and-dirty way to estimate.
Typically, we can determine download time by taking the file size (converted into bits) and dividing it by the speed of your internet . For instance, my 1GB FiOS connection should take about 28 minutes to download. Meanwhile, someone on a 300 Mbps plan might need over an hour and a half to install the same file.
However, this doesn't account for real-world factors such as network congestion and location, so think of it as more of a ballpark estimate. You're better off preloading as soon as possible, so no matter how long it takes, it'll be loaded day before November 19 rolls around.
Preorders began back in June , but you can still preorder Grand Theft Auto 6 so you can get started on preloading the game. You'll have to decide which version of the game you want to buy—the $80 Standard Edition or the $100 Ultimate Edition. Don't worry, if you opt for the Standard Edition, you can always upgrade later.

articles.title_orig: Rewards platform Bilt announces 'next evolution' for American consumers, small businesses
articles.title_zh: Rewards platform Bilt announces 'next evolution' for American consumers, small businesses
articles.content_orig:
Bilt unveiled its transformed Neighborhood OS on Tuesday. ( Bilt )
Bilt, best known for helping renters earn rewards on housing payments, is expanding into local commerce with a new artificial intelligence platform aimed at helping businesses attract customers while giving consumers more ways to earn rewards close to home.
The company announced Tuesday that it is launching "Bilt Neighborhood OS," which connects with existing business systems for reservations, payments, customer management and loyalty programs to help merchants reach nearby customers, personalize offers and track spending.
For consumers, the expansion could mean earning rewards and receiving personalized offers at more restaurants, retailers and other businesses they visit near home. For merchants, it could mean reaching new customers without replacing their existing technology.
Bilt describes the launch as the "next evolution" of its business, expanding the rewards network it built around housing payments into a broader platform connecting consumers, neighborhood merchants and larger organizations.
"The last tech revolution transformed how businesses sell online, but it largely left behind the businesses that make our neighborhoods special," Bilt founder and CEO Ankur Jain said in a statement.
GOOGLE EXPANDS VOLUNTARY BUYOUTS TO 5 COUNTRIES AS AI SPENDING FUELS COST CUTS
The move builds on Bilt's network of more than 8.2 million members, who generated over $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local businesses over the past 12 months, the company said.
Launched in 2021, Bilt now reaches approximately one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year.
Bilt founder and CEO Ankur Jain gave details on Neighborhood OS to Fox News Digital. (Bilt)
The expansion includes two offerings through Bilt for Business: Neighborhood OS, which uses AI to help merchants attract customers, build loyalty and manage business activities, and Bilt Membership Platform, which allows organizations across sports , travel, hospitality, workplaces and financial services to create branded membership programs or extend existing rewards into local communities.
A neighborhood restaurant, for example, could use Neighborhood OS to identify potential customers, send targeted offers, recognize returning guests and automatically apply rewards through its existing point-of-sale system.
Bilt says its AI agents completed more than 2 million real-world actions across more than 29,000 businesses during the past 30 days, with 91% of those actions completed without human intervention.
The platform also includes Neighborhood ID, which Bilt describes as a privacy-preserving system for connecting customer experiences without exchanging raw customer data, and Neighborhood Pass, which allows eligible members to access personalized rewards and benefits at participating businesses.
To expand its reach, Bilt is partnering with payment and commerce companies including Verifone, Clover from Fiserv, Shift4, OpenTable and Grubhub. The partnerships could eventually make Neighborhood OS available to millions of merchants, with integrations and capabilities rolling out in phases beginning in 2027.
Bilt and Hyatt say they are also looking at how World of Hyatt members could be rewarded through neighborhood experiences with Bilt Neighborhood OS. Bilt added that it will partner with Meta in 2027 to provide education and business resources to small-business owners.
The platform is also giving $100,000 to the community development organization Local Initiatives Support Corporation.
"Our partnership with Bilt will test new ways to connect financial coaching and resources with people's housing goals, including pathways to homeownership, with the goal of reaching more individuals, families, and communities across the country," said Valerie White, head of National Housing Strategic Initiatives at Local Initiatives Support Corporation.
The company is targeting a sizable share of consumer spending. Bilt estimates that approximately $6.6 trillion in annual US retail and food-services spending occurs in person.
Its inaugural State of the Neighborhood study, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global and commissioned by Bilt, surveyed 6,591 US adults. It found that two-thirds conduct at least 80% of their everyday spending within their neighborhood, while the median consumer shops within 15 miles of home.
The survey also found that 95% of respondents would try a local business at least once if they could earn points or rewards there, while 87% said rewards would make them more likely to shop at a local business more frequently.
Bilt is also expanding into professional sports, with the Phoenix Suns, Phoenix Mercury, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans, Houston Comets and Sacramento Kings planning branded fan loyalty experiences that could reward customers inside and outside stadiums, with phased launches beginning in 2027.
The effort follows Bilt's $300 million acquisition of loyalty technology company LAVA, whose technology supports programs for 56 professional sports teams, according to the company. Bilt is also working with Mastercard to extend cardholder rewards into participating neighborhood businesses.
Ankur Jain and Brian Kelly attend the Bilt Rewards Launch Party at Equinox Hotel New York at Hudson Yards on June 22, 2021, in New York City. (Sean Zanni/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
Jain said Bilt's focus is on helping smaller businesses compete in an increasingly technology-driven economy.
"Our number-one goal is to grow small business," Jain told Fox News Digital. He said the company wants to empower small businesses to "grow and win against large companies that have had an unfair advantage on them."
Jain also warned that efforts to restrict AI development could hurt smaller companies that stand to benefit from the technology.

"If you hamper AI, you're hurting small business across America," he said. "AI is going to be a great democratizing force in Congress."

articles.title_orig: How does Roshi Joan Halifax make sense of her Buddhist life?
articles.title_zh: How does Roshi Joan Halifax make sense of her Buddhist life?
articles.content_orig:
Joan Halifax. Photo by Kodo Noah Roen
Six weeks after two open-heart surgeries in 12 days, Roshi Joan Halifax invited me for a visit. She was recovering, but feeling ‘weak as a kitten’. When I’d last seen her, three or four years earlier, her hair had been shorn in a Zen tonsure; now it hung in a lush, grey-streaked braid to the middle of her back. She was pale and short of breath.
As a physician and her friend, I was reluctant to press on with the interview, but she wanted to begin. She was staying with Wendy Lau, her close friend, an emergency physician and Zen priest whose home overlooks Upaya, the Zen centre Halifax established in 1990 in the foothills above Santa Fe in New Mexico. We sat on Lau’s back porch, drinking tea.
Halifax is a medical anthropologist, a Buddhist teacher and a caregiver to the dying, who has worked with the suffering of others for more than 50 years: in burn units and jail clinics, in remote Himalayan villages, at the bedsides of people for whom there was nothing left to cure. She learned that the qualities that drew her there could also pull her under, and more than once they did. When she found her way back, it was Buddhist practice that helped her remain steady enough to help.
Halifax had almost died. She had gone into the operating room at Stanford cheerful, she told me – upbeat, confident. Surgeons repaired her heart’s mitral valve. Coming out of anaesthesia, intubated, she was certain the tube was positioned incorrectly. She couldn’t speak, so she made writing motions until someone put a pen in her hand, and – stoned, half-conscious – she wrote glottis . Wendy Lau understood. They fixed it.
Then came what she called the worst 12 days of her life. The valve replacement was failing. Her blood pressure plunged; she bled internally; she had a dangerous arrhythmia, and had to be shocked to restore a normal heart rhythm. ‘Death is easier than this,’ she told Lau. She meant it. ‘I actually wanted to die,’ she said. ‘I just was so sick.’
She was still on a gurney from the latest resuscitative shock when the surgeon appeared in his scrubs and told her: ‘We have to take you back in.’
‘I had a moment of Yikes! ’ she told me.
In the intensive care unit after the second operation, she awoke convinced she was hanging upside down against a wall of moss. A warmth enveloped her chest and expanded, and kept expanding, into utter bliss. Then a male voice said: ‘You’re not done with your work yet,’ and she found herself back against the moss-covered wall. The cycle began again. ‘My recognition was: this is death. It’s fine,’ Halifax said.
Halifax has spent much of her life crossing thresholds, sometimes knowingly and sometimes not, and in the process delivering a grittier, more hands-on and help-oriented form of Buddhism to the West. Now aged 84, facing her own mortality, she names the charnel grounds where she practised her art: refugee camps, prisons, cancer wards, war zones. To that list she adds one more. ‘My latest charnel ground was being hospitalised for this heart surgery,’ she said.
H alifax’s first encounter with illness had come 80 years earlier. Aged four, she woke one morning unable to see and partially paralysed on her left side. She remembers feeling her way along the wall into her parents’ bedroom. Later, when a doctor picked her up in his convertible, she knew the top was down only from the wind.
She spent much of the next couple of years in bed with polio, away from other children. ‘I discovered that I had a spiritual life, an inner life,’ she said. Even now, she can walk through a building in her mind, imagining its rooms and passages, ‘because that’s what I did when I was four.’
Her parents hired Lila Robinson, a local Black woman, to care for her, keep house and cook. The Halifaxes lived in Coral Gables in Florida, a restricted, all-white enclave where neither Jews nor African Americans were allowed to live. Robinson and her three daughters lived across the railroad tracks in West Coconut Grove, then known as ‘Coloured Town’, in what Halifax called a ‘concrete monster’ – one of the mould-filled, roach-infested semi-high-rises baking in the Florida heat. To Halifax, Robinson was ‘the most incredibly kind person in the world, a manifestation of unconditional love and brightness – the woman who raised me.’
As Halifax recovered, she sometimes rode with her father to pick up Robinson. The journey carried her between ‘two different universes’: one had a country club and an all-white school, and the other: understocked shops, tired cars, good music and warmth. She saw the gulf between the two but was not entirely convinced that hers was the better world. Looking back, she traced her attraction to places of suffering to that early collision of inequality and love.
‘You could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that’
At the H Sophie Newcomb women’s college of Tulane University in New Orleans, the disparity Halifax had registered as a child became something she could act on. It was 1960 and, with the civil rights movement gathering force around her, she joined protests and the fight for racial justice. ‘There was a whole cadre of us who felt that racism was abhorrent,’ she said.
Through that work, Halifax met Hodding Carter II, the progressive Southern newspaper editor who had established the Delta Democrat-Times in Greenville, Mississippi. Carter was going blind. ‘For a time, I became his kind of eyes and feet and hands,’ Halifax said – his assistant in civil rights activities. Carter and his wife supported her, but her activism put her at odds with Tulane. ‘I graduated early from Tulane with Tulane’s help, so to speak,’ she recalled. ‘They really wanted me out of the system.’
In 1963, she left for New York, where her civil rights work opened into a wider world of artists, musicians, filmmakers and political activists. There she met Alan Lomax, the folklorist and ethnomusicologist whose field recordings of folk, jazz and blues musicians had taken him around the world. His project studied music, dance and language across cultures. The work carried her from a huge computer in a university basement to field trips in Morocco, the Bahamas and rural Arkansas. ‘I was in anthropology heaven,’ she recalled. ‘I just wanted to learn everything about anthropology that I possibly could.’
Two years later, a different kind of encounter opened a path inward. Halifax heard the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh speak when he came to New York to urge an end to the bombing of his country through the calm of his Buddhist practice. Halifax was then ‘angry all the time’ – at the war, racism, the government and the suffering around her. She understood that ‘you could be both contemplative and a social activist. I want to be like that,’ she thought. But for almost a decade, she remained a ‘book Buddhist’, absorbing what she could from reading alone.
Joan Halifax and her Pentax, photographed by Mark Moskowitz in Paris, 1968, from Flickr
For now, her focus was anthropology. By 1968, she was in Paris, indexing ethnographic films at the Musée de l’Homme. There she met Germaine Dieterlen, a French anthropologist who had spent more than 20 years among the Dogon people of central Mali. Dieterlen told Halifax that the Dogon were midway through the Sigui, a seven-year cycle of ceremonies moving through 289 villages and held only once about every 60 years. Most Dogon would attend just one Segui in a lifetime. To Halifax, it was a rite of passage that ‘reconsecrated an entire culture’.
The attraction was also personal. Robinson’s family had roots in the Bahamas and, farther back, in Africa; her grandmother had been a slave. Halifax knew little more – not when the family had been taken, nor from where. ‘I really wanted to go to Africa,’ she told me, ‘to understand the cultural roots of this woman who had raised me.’

Wang Junwei, director of the Academic and Editorial Committee of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said in his keynote speech that seeking common ground while preserving differences and pursuing cooperation for mutual benefit are important principles guiding China's approach to international relations and valuable experience in ensuring the steady development of China-Europe relations. These principles will continue to play a guiding role in cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European countries (CEEC) in the future, he said.
In her welcome remarks, Chinese Ambassador to Bulgaria Dai Qingli said that as long as China and Europe uphold mutual respect and engage in equal-footed consultations, both sides will be able to find solutions to problems and continuously expand the scope for mutually beneficial cooperation.
Nataliya Kiselova, former president of the National Assembly of Bulgaria, said in her remarks that the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC demonstrated the CPC leadership's courage to uphold the truth and curb abuses of power, and its determination to continue consolidating its position as the core of leadership in Chinese society.

articles.content_orig:
Rockstar Games’ latest batch of GTA VI screenshots unveils Kodak Black as an in-game NPC
The rapper is pictured gripping a cup stamped with the logo of Jack of Hearts, a club that has surfaced repeatedly across the game’s marketing
The reveal has intensified theories that other real-world artists, including Travis Scott, could make their own cameos
The clue that matters most is sitting in his hand. Zoom in on the shot and Kodak Black is holding a cup branded with the Jack of Hearts logo, tying him directly to one of GTA VI’s in-game clubs. Jack of Hearts has been a recurring presence throughout Rockstar’s promotional rollout, and Travis Scott even worked the venue’s name into “RHYNO,” a track he recorded specifically for the game’s soundtrack.
That connection is fueling the bigger question. Fans have long suspected the club would serve as a hub for recognizable artists, and a confirmed Kodak Black sighting makes the theory much harder to dismiss. Scott is the obvious next candidate, though any of the rappers lined up for the official soundtrack could plausibly surface inside the venue. Rockstar has not confirmed any additional appearances.
There is also a strong hometown logic to the casting. Kodak Black hails from Pompano Beach, Florida, and GTA VI’s state of Leonida is the series’ take on Florida, making him a natural fit for the setting.
The franchise has a track record that backs up the speculation. GTA Online’s 2018 After Hours update turned real DJs including Solomun, Tale Of Us, Dixon and The Black Madonna into resident performers at player-owned nightclubs, a template that maps neatly onto a venue like Jack of Heart. Rockstar pushed the idea further in 2021 with The Contract , which cast Dr. Dre as himself at the center of a full storyline. Going back even earlier, GTA: San Andreas enlisted rappers such as Ice-T to voice characters, including the fictional rap star Madd Dogg.
Check out the screenshot above. GTA VI is live November 19.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yields Turn Higher on Fed’s Waller Comments; Eurozone Bond Yields Fall
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yields Turn Higher on Fed’s Waller Comments; Eurozone Bond Yields Fall
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields jumped on Tuesday after the U.S. consumer price index data for October came in hotter than expected .
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Fed rate decisions, added more than 15 basis points, to 4.698%. Yields on the 10-year Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, car loans and credit card rates — climbed more than 7 basis points to 4.938%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield, more sensitive to geopolitical developments, rose more than 3 basis points at 5.29%.
One basis point equals 0.01% or 1/100 th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The consumer price index for October grew 0.4%, more than the 0.3% expected from economists polled by Dow Jones and down from the 0.6% growth in September.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, gained 0.3%. Economists had expected a 0.2% gain on the month. The reading was in line with September's 0.3% rise.
The report came after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he would support "more robust action" if inflation readings are higher than expected.
"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting," Waller said in London at a central bank conference hosted by the Bank of England. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said the hot CPI numbers signal that Fed hikes could spill into 2027.
"The Fed could push for a more-aggressive tightening cycle with CPI continuing to print strong," she said. "A December hike is our firm base case despite wider AI jitters, and stubborn inflation means we cannot rule out further hikes in 2027."
Oil prices dipped further on Tuesday morning, with Brent crude falling below $90 a barrel for the first time since August. This comes on the back of President Donald Trump's comments that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon" as he played down the prospect of further strikes in the region.
Tuesday's CPI data, together with wholesale inflation numbers due Friday, may shape the Federal Reserve's future decisions on interest rates in the U.S. Markets have already largely priced in a 25 basis point hike in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch .
It comes after U.S. employment data came in considerably stronger than Wall Street was expecting last week, with 165,000 jobs added in October, more than double forecasts.
