articles.title_orig: Mini Review: Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell
articles.title_zh: Mini Review: Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell
articles.content_orig:
Warhammer Survivors is exactly what its name suggests: a Warhammer reskin of Vampire Survivors .
Developed by licensed Warhammer studio Auroch Digital, with Vampire Survivors creator poncle partnering on the project, it's a fantastic, heartfelt adaptation right out of the gate.
Indeed, it's immediately obvious that an awful lot of care has been taken in providing poncle's world-beating gameplay formula with a fresh coat of paint. The Warhammer settings, characters, enemies, and weapons are all there — but the game also relishes in dishing out smaller references to Games Workshop's immensely popular fiction.
In particular, I was left pleasantly surprised by how often Warhammer Survivors pays tribute to the property's tabletop identity. Numerous playable characters, for example, are unlocked by finding miniature figure paints scattered across maps.
Meanwhile, power ups can include rolling damage dice — actual dice — across the battlefield, crushing your foes in the process. You can even drop giant blast radius templates on top of your enemies if you're lucky.
What I'm saying is that Auroch Digital and poncle clearly had loads of fun with this one — it's not just a simple copy and paste job that takes advantage of the Warhammer name.
Oh, and it's basically two games in one. On the main menu, you can pick between Warhammer's dark sci-fi 40,000 setting, and its high fantasy Age of Sigmar setting. Each comes with its own character roster, maps, enemy factions, objectives, upgrades, and everything else, making for a seriously robust package.
Gameplay-wise, the title offers a slight twist on the absurdly addictive Survivors structure. Stages have a 25-minute time limit instead of 30, and I'd say there's a larger emphasis on tactical thinking.
That's because specialised opponents are more prevalent, forcing you to weave your way through the hordes in a more methodical manner. At least, until you rack up so many super-powered upgrades that anything in your path just evaporates anyway.
Yep, that same progression curve that makes Vampire Survivors so insanely moreish is alive and well here, although I do think it takes a little longer to hit those truly chaotic highs because of the aforementioned tweaks.
All in all, Warhammer Survivors perfectly melds Games Workshop's property with poncle's timeless formula, resulting in another exceptional roguelike experience.
Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.

By JO MACFARLANE, HEALTH REPORTER
Published: 02:01 EST, 18 October 2026 | Updated: 05:58 EST, 26 October 2026
Sitting in the park with her grandchildren one afternoon, Becky Tucker decided to overhaul her life.
As the four of them played and ran around, Becky, then 48, simply lacked the energy to join in. It was, she says now, a wake-up call.
The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had been struggling with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes as perimenopause took hold.
And for as long as she could remember, she had experienced intense, debilitating migraines for a week every month, linked to her menstrual cycle.
She was also significantly overweight – something she had struggled with her whole life. At more than 13 stone and with a BMI of 29 – bordering on obese – Becky had spent the previous 25 years on various weight-loss plans.
They'd worked, to begin with, but then she piled on the pounds again when she returned to her usual diet of chocolate bars and what she calls 'beige stodge'.
It will be a familiar scenario to many in midlife – the pounds creep on until it no longer feels possible to shift them.
But three years on, it is no exaggeration to say that Becky is transformed. Indeed, as our photos show so clearly, she is almost unrecognisable. Fizzing with energy and an astonishing four stone lighter, she says she feels like a different woman.
Becky Tucker shed four stone by following the ZOE diet. The risk management consultant from Poole, Dorset, had  previously struggled with fatigue, anxiety, mood swings and hot flushes
At more than 13 stone and with a BMI of 29 – bordering on obese – Becky had spent the previous 25 years on various weight-loss plans

Her enviably slender figure has shrunk by more than four dress sizes, from a 16 to an 8 or 10. Her near-lifelong migraines have vanished, as have those limiting menopause symptoms.
And most importantly of all? She is now running around the park with her grandchildren, no longer stuck on a bench at the sidelines.
But what is extraordinary is that Becky achieved it – and she says this almost apologetically – 'without really trying'.
There was no restrictive diet, no calorie counting, and no pangs of hunger. Instead, Becky overhauled her diet with the help of gut health science company ZOE, co-founded by Professor Tim Spector, the scientist at the forefront of discoveries in diet and gut health and their impact on our overall health – and, research increasingly suggests, our mood.
Hi, I'm Professor Tim Spector, a medical scientist at King's College London, co-founder of ZOE and author of Good Mood Food.
I've spent decades researching how the food we eat affects our weight, mood and brain health. Now I'd like to share what I've discovered with you.
My exclusive six-week ZOE diet plan will show you how to eat your way to better health, with delicious recipes, simple changes and no calorie counting.
You could even lose up to a stone in time for the Christmas party season. And for DailyMail+ subscribers, it's completely free.

Research by Professor Spector, an honorary consulting physician and expert in epidemiology at King's College London, suggests that simple changes to our food choices can have remarkable benefits – from helping us lose weight without going hungry to improving our mood, boosting energy and potentially protecting our brains against the effects of ageing.
And now, in an exclusive new six-week newsletter series launching on Monday, October 26, the Daily Mail's readers can discover how to put his research into practice – with the chance to feel happier and healthier within days, and potentially as a bonus even lose up to a stone in time for Christmas.
Based on Professor Spector’s research at ZOE, and including recipes from his new cookbook Good Mood Food, the series will guide you, step-by-step, through a new way of eating that could transform not just your waistline, but most importantly how you feel every day.
You'll discover the surprisingly simple foods that nourish the trillions of bacteria living in your gut, why these microbes may hold the key to better mood and brain health, and how to feed them.
We'll show you what to put in your shopping basket – and what to leave on the shelves – and how to build delicious, filling meals.
There will be exclusive recipes, from hearty breakfasts and satisfying dinners to indulgent desserts, along with expert advice on eating to support your mood and thinking as you get older.
Halfway through, Professor Spector will make a live appearance on dailymail.com to answer readers' questions and talk about his cookbook.
And as Christmas approaches he'll reveal how to enjoy your favourite festive foods without undoing all your hard work – and, crucially, how to make these changes stick for life.
Indeed, research by Professor Spector's gut health company ZOE found that 35 per cent of around 5,000 participants lost at least 5 per cent of their body weight in just three months.
Their approach to diet has become a global phenomenon, refined through years of research involving hundreds of thousands of people.
Although more personalised recommendations are available to ZOE subscribers, anyone can follow the basic principles, for free.
Becky overhauled her diet with the help of nutrition science company ZOE, co-founded by Professor Tim Spector, the scientist at the forefront of discoveries in diet and gut health
These include eating 30 different plants a week, by making simple tweaks such as sprinkling seeds, nuts or fresh herbs over a salad or soup, or adding chopped fruit or greens to a plate.
Professor Spector encourages dieters to swap meat, particularly processed meat such as sausages, bacon and salami, for plant-based proteins including beans, lentils and chickpeas, and to aim for at least 30g of fibre a day.
However, chicken, lean meat and especially oily fish can still be enjoyed as part of his approach.
Ultra-processed foods, or UPFs – industrially-produced foods lacking in nutrients and containing cosmetic additives designed to make food irresistible to eat – are discouraged.
Instead, meals should be based on whole foods, with a rainbow of different-coloured plants to maximise nutrients.
'Studies have found that people who eat healthy diets, full of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, significantly improve their mood,' Professor Spector says.
'On the other hand, people who eat the most UPFs such as crisps, biscuits, sausages, sugary soft drinks, chicken nuggets and sugary cereal, have the biggest risk of mental health problems and dementia.
'When people have moderate depression, giving them a gut-friendly diet can improve or reverse symptoms in a significant proportion of them.'
Despite this, processed foods such as baked beans, Weetabix and high-fibre or seeded bread are on the menu.
Fermented foods, including natural yogurt, sourdough bread, kefir, sauerkraut, kombucha and kimchi, also have a role to play, as do dark chocolate and peanut butter. Most of these feature in the cookbook.
'It's not about restriction or cutting out all processed foods,' he explains, 'it's about cutting back on the worst unhealthy ultra-processed foods and replacing them with real whole plants'.
Eating more whole foods increases fibre intake – nine in ten Britons fail to get the recommended 30g a day, which can help protect against bowel cancer, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
All ZOE studies to date have shown improvements in mood and energy within the first two weeks in the majority of people.
High-fibre foods also make you feel fuller for longer and can stimulate the release of GLP-1, the appetite-regulating hormone mimicked by weight-loss drugs.
Becky, now 52, is proof of how powerful these changes can be – with benefits she never expected.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang lobbied ‘very good friend’ Trump for more Nvidia sales to China while ‘caught in Beijing’s honeytrap’
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made himself President Trump’s “very good friend” and lobbied the administration to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China while he was allegedly ensnared in a Chinese honeytrap, a timeline of his reported relationship with Alice Huang shows.
The $150 billion AI boss appeared in loved-up snaps with accused communist spy Alice Huang last year — and then weeks later personally pitched Trump at the White House on relaxing export restrictions for the company’s chips.
Huang missed Trump’s second inauguration, but then more than made up for it with a $25 million donation to the president’s ballroom project.
The 63-year-old appeared at a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025, where he pushed to lift chip restrictions that had just been imposed. There were at least three documented meetings between Trump and Huang where the administration responded with policy changes that made it easier for Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
China hawks have long pushed to restrict the most cutting edge chips from the communist regime in an attempt to blunt its technological advances and stymie its attempts to overtake the US on AI.
Huang, for his part, had lobbied and spoken out against restrictions since the Biden administration first imposed limits in 2022. Additionally, selling more chips to the world’s second largest economy could only help Nvidia’s bottom line.
But all the while, Huang — who has been married to college sweetheart Lori for more than 40 years — was meeting with 42-year-old Alice. In May 2025, they were spotted at dinner together during Taiwan’s top tech expo, where she looked at him adoringly and affectionately touched his arm as they sat with other tech honchos.
Alice Huang — a TV host, turned banker, turned executive at the Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed — met Jensen Huang (no relation) in early 2024, according to reports. Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars in chips from Nvidia for data centers in Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
Separately, the firm — backed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba — is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips to China. The US government is probing reports that 50,000 chips sold to Megaspeed were seemingly missing following an audit.
Nvidia reportedly intervened in that probe, according to Bloomberg.
The Chinese government denies allegations of a honeypot spy scheme. Megaspeed also denies allegations of wrongdoing.
Trump himself has downplayed Huang’s admission of infidelity and Nvidia’s board said the company, which has no succession plan for replacing Huang, had full confidence in him, even as it announced it was investigating the claims.
On Monday, Trump said he called to check on Huang after he admitted cheating on his wife and apologized to his family.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right,” Trump said at the White House. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really believe him.”
The president and the Nvidia “have become good friends,” a source close to them told The Post.
Huang has made himself an integral part of the US economy. Nvidia reached a historic $5.5 trillion in valuation in May 2026, beating out Apple at the time as the most valuable public company in the entire world. It is both the world’s most important chipmaker, and the locus around which the AI boom spins. It uses the profits from its sales to help fund AI companies building out data centers, spurring further demand for its products.
By some accounts the AI boom is expected to account for up to 4% of all US economic activity this year, and Nvidia’s revenues alone up to 1%.
Trump personally hailed Nvidia’s latest quarter record sales of $96.2 billion in September, up 106% from last year.
Huang notably traveled with the president during his trip to China last May, with Trump even going as far as to personally invite the Nvidia boss to ride with him on Air Force One.
When Huang couldn’t make it to Washington DC in time for departure, he took his private plane to Alaska to join the president during his refueling stop in Anchorage.
Dressed in his signature black leather jacket and carrying only a backpack, Jensen boarded the presidential plane alone, without an entourage, pausing to speak with Trump’s son Eric, who was also on the trip, as he boarded.
Huang and his wife were seated at the head table with the president and first lady Melania Trump at the September state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping . Trump was personally involved in selecting the guest list for that dinner, a source familiar with the planning told The Post.
Along with the gains for his company, Huang’s relationship with Trump reportedly came with some perks of power.
Huang called the president when his invitation to the April state dinner for King Charles arrived without a plus one, according to a source. The billionaire CEO wanted to bring his wife to the dinner.
When White House staff told him there were no plus ones, he called Trump and made a personal appeal, getting Lori Huang on the list and bumping a senior administration official off of it to make room for her, multiple administration sources told The Post.
Huang has two grown children with his wife, Spencer and Madison, who both work in their father’s company.
The family has a $38 million home in San Francisco , with Nvidia spending nearly $4 million in fiscal 2026 on services for Huang that included home security, protection during personal travel, consulting and drivers, according to its May proxy filing.
Huang has remained close to Trump, literally, traveling to the Middle East for Trump’s visit to Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates in May 2025, then to London to join the president at Windsor Castle for a state dinner with King Charles that September.
Trump, at a meeting with then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer during that visit, saw the CEO in the audience and teasingly told him: “You’re taking over the world Jensen. I don’t know what you’re doing here. I hope you’re right.”
He also had a prime seat at Trump’s side at the September 29th meeting on AI policy , alongside other technology executives. And the president awarded him the National Medal of Science last month.
Huang and Trump remained close friends despite the warning signs about the Nvidia boss’ relationship with Alice, which one tech company flagged to the Commerce Department last summer.
“The White House has known how suspicious Ms. Huang, and her corporate network, is since last summer,” a source familiar with the case told The Post. “And Jensen has repeatedly lied about his relationship with Ms. Huang.”
Culper Research also published a report titled “NVIDIA (NVDA): The China Problem” in May 2026, which specifically warned about the concerning rumors about Nvidia’s chief executive and Alice.
Alice had been under investigation since the Biden administration and believed to have been recruited as an asset for China’s feared Ministry of State Security.
The Commerce Department first flagged Alice following her sudden rise to the top of Megaspeed in 2023.
The concerns were troubling enough that Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed back on letting Huang attend the China state dinner with Trump, the source added.
Little is known about the alleged spy’s private life, but before entering the world of finance, Alice had worked as a reporter for CCTV, the national broadcaster of the Chinese state, and Hunan TV, a regional broadcaster in central China, according to her LinkedIn biography.
Local reports claimed Alice is married to former Shanghai Hexi chairman Kang Wei — a former business partner, whose firm was fined $2.7M and censured by the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.
Trump told reporters in the White House Monday, after a meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, that "We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon."
"Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump said, citing the destruction of its navy and surging inflation that he said has hollowed out its economy.
Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait would "prefer the status quo" which involves maintaining the naval blockade against Iran and "Operation Iron Gate" — a task force announced on Saturday aimed at preventing Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials — Trump said in a Truth Social post.
He reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to have a nuclear weapon and kept the door open for potentially resuming strikes should circumstances change. "America is 'docked and loaded' and ready to go," he said, though caveating that new strikes were "quite unlikely."
The conflict, now in its ninth month, has driven a surge in fuel prices, hitting nearly every sector of the global economy.
The U.S. had reportedly planned for a potential increase in naval forces in the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections, with Trump hinting at escalating the conflict after the results.
The administration has since toned down the war rhetoric after bruising midterm election results that saw Republicans lose both chambers of Congress as voters expressed frustration with soaring living costs stemming from the war.
A diplomat briefed on the Qatar meeting told Axios that Trump told Al Thani that he wanted a deal and would give talks a chance, but could reverse course if Iran does not take the negotiations seriously.
Iran has put forward a two-day proposal to the U.S. via Qatari mediators, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official , demanding lifting of the sanctions imposed on Tehran and a new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington was reviewing the proposal, according to the report.
Iranian officials have disputed that talks with Washington were underway. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, reportedly said that Washington should stop "manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."
Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday on the prospect of de-escalation, extending losses from the previous day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate dropped over 1% to $85.8 per barrel, after sliding more than 4% in the prior session. Brent futures dropped more than 1% to $91.56 a barrel, hovering near 10-week low levels.

articles.title_zh: Brent at $90 a Barrel as Trump Plays Down Need For Further Iran Strikes
articles.content_orig:
Brent crude drops below $90 and markets climb after president downplays prospect of further strikes
Business live – latest updates
Oil prices have fallen to the lowest level since late August while stock markets climbed higher, as markets reacted with relief to Donald Trump saying that the war on Iran is “effectively over” .
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell nearly 3% to $89.66, the lowest since 31 August, on Tuesday morning, after the US president downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”. The fall came after a near 6% drop on Monday on signs that the conflict might be nearing an end.
Europe’s benchmark Stoxx 600 index gained 0.9% to 662.54, hovering near a record high, which it had hit in early August on hopes for a peace deal in the Middle East.
Airline stocks rose amid hopes that easing tensions could lead to lower fuel costs, with Lufthansa 1.8% ahead and Air France-KLM up 1.2%.
In London, the FTSE 100 index climbed 45 points, or 0.4%, to 10,828. The oil companies BP and Shell were the biggest losers, down 1.7% and 1.5% respectively.
During a White House press conference, Trump said Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and an escalation was not needed.
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at the trading platform Capital.com, said: “Global markets are extending their recovery this morning after Wall Street recorded a strong session that was relatively broad-based, supported by a sharp decline in oil prices and renewed buying in technology stocks.”
However, the US Federal Reserve will want more evidence of slowing inflation, she said. The latest US inflation data for October will be released at 1.30pm GMT.
Hathorn added: “Ultimately, markets are benefiting from an improvement in the geopolitical outlook, but the underlying macroeconomic and corporate risks remain unresolved. Lower energy prices could help ease inflation expectations, but the Fed will need evidence of broader disinflation before reconsidering its policy stance.

“The key question is whether today’s inflation figures support the recovery or remind investors that resilient economic growth and persistent price pressures could keep borrowing costs elevated for longer. With technology valuations still sensitive to yields, another inflation surprise could quickly bring volatility back into focus.”
Drivers will hope the fall in wholesale oil prices continues to feed through to prices at the pump.
The AA said on Monday at the average UK petrol price has fallen 5p a litre since early October, to 169.7p a litre, and that wholesale markets indicated that another 10p reduction should be on the way.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s China Spy Fallout Deepens: Report Says Moonshot AI Accessed NVDA’s Advanced Chips Despite Export Controls
articles.content_orig:
By ANDREW JEHRING, CHIEF FOREIGN CORRESPONDENT and JOHN-PAUL FORD ROJAS, DEPUTY BUSINESS EDITOR
Published: 19:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 22:08 EST, 9 November 2026
The Chinese 'spy' accused of honey-trapping the boss of the world's biggest AI chip firm had bragged that she could secure his firm's technology despite a US export ban.
Alice Huang pitched a deal to Beijing investors to secure Nvidia's coveted graphics processing units (GPUs) last year.
Ms Huang said she had 'no problem securing GPUs', the Financial Times reported, even though Chinese firms are barred from obtaining them by the US.
She did not disclose her relationship with Nvidia's married chief executive Jensen Huang, who is no relation, during the investment pitch for a data centre project in Singapore .
Washington imposed strict limits on the US firm's exports to thwart attempts by Chinese president Xi Jinping to become the leading AI superpower by 2030.
Nvidia went into meltdown on Monday after Mr Huang admitted having an affair with Ms Huang months after she was declared a Chinese spy by US intelligence.
On Sunday, the 63-year-old said in a memo to staff: 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.'
The company has commissioned an independent probe into the affair. It lost around £292billion of its value – or 9 per cent – in minutes on Monday, equal to the combined value of HSBC and Barclays. Its shares recovered, but it was still down by 4 per cent by the evening, making it worth around £3trillion.
Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang is pictured at a party with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang in June 2024
Mr Huang admitted he was 'unfaithful' to his wife, Lori Huang, who he is pictured with her during a visit to the White House on September 24
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies.
Within a year the previously dormant firm became the largest buyer of Nvidia's chips in south-east Asia. Weeks before they started purchasing the chips she was seen drinking whisky with Taiwan-born American businessman Mr Huang in Taipei – the first known pictures of them together.
Megaspeed's imports topped £3.6billion as it opened facilities across south-east Asia and rented the firm's technology to the Chinese tech giant Alibaba.
The investments set off alarm bells in Washington and Ms Huang was placed under surveillance at the end of 2024. Earlier this year she was named as a spy in a US intelligence report.
However, Donald Trump – a close ally of Mr Huang – did nothing, the New York Times reported.
Theresa Fallon, director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies in Brussels, said: 'It is always amazing to see how so-called intelligent people fall for a Chinese honey-trap.'
Rush Doshi, an assistant security studies professor at Georgetown University in Washington, said: 'If the reporting is right, this is the most significant story in US-China policy in years.
'If the US knew Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese spy and looked the other way, all while that spy ran a company backdooring US compute to China, it warrants a Congressional investigation.'
America restricted firms from exporting advanced Nvidia chips to China in 2022, but some smuggled them illegally over the border. Others legally set up businesses that buy large numbers of chips to build data centres in south-east Asia that serve Chinese firms.
Ms Huang apparently worked as a Chinese state TV reporter and had a stint in private equity before she formed Megaspeed International in 2023, according to unverified internet biographies
Mr Huang is pictured with President Donald Trump last month
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, appeared to be a middle man, buying Nvidia chips and providing computing power to Chinese firms operating outside the country. However, it was suspected of smuggling the tech into China.
Mr Huang lobbied Mr Trump to relax export laws on chips, and when a US delegation visited China last May he was initially left off the list due to concerns about his 'influence on the President's policy of only lightly regulating AI'.
Silicon Valley giants defended the tech tycoon last night. Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, a tech investment firm, tweeted that Mr Huang was 'irreplaceable for America's AI leadership', adding: 'My guess is there was no bad intention.' SpaceX boss Elon Musk said: 'I agree.'
Wall Street hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said: 'Jensen Huang is human. And he is an incredible human... even incredible humans make mistakes.'
China denied Ms Huang was a spy and accused the US of 'groundless smears and slanders'.
Nvidia said it 'prioritises US national and economic security' but 'has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
It added that Mr Huang was co-operating with its investigation and would remain as chief executive pending the review.

articles.title_zh: What we know about the mystery woman at the center of Nvidia's spy scandal
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares edged higher in premarket trading Tuesday as investors continued to weigh the potential fallout from CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares closed more than 4% lower on Monday, the day after Huang told staff in an email that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife and had "fallen short" of his responsibilities as CEO.
He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed , an Nvidia customer. The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that U.S. officials had concluded she was "a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing" and "possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China."
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating .
"I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago," Trump told reporters at the White House . "We'll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape."
The stock was trading 1.8% higher as of 4:40 a.m. ET.

Nintendo has released a new firmware update for the Switch 2 this week, bumping it up to Version 23.5.0 .
Most notably, it's added support for "gifting" eShop products to a Nintendo Account family group member. This is an "upcoming feature" and is scheduled to go live on 17th November 2026 .
Apart from this, there's now also the ability to configure accessibility settings during the first-time setup, and there are some language updates. A Switch 1 update is out today as well, adding gifting feature support, and some general adjustments & fixes.
Here are the full patch notes for Version 23.5.0, courtesy of Nintendo's official support page:
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Nintendo goes into some more detail about the gifting feature on its website , explaining how it can be used to give a child or family member a game for a special occasion.
You can send a gift by selecting the "Give as a Gift" option on an eShop product page, and even choose your gift wrap colour. From there, all the recipient has to do is accept the gift, and they can then play it.
The Version 23.5.0 update has also supposedly patched the recently discovered jailbreak exploit . You can find out more about this in our previous story . This latest update also follows a major Switch 2 system update (Version 23.0.0) in September, which added VRR for TV mode and much more.

articles.title_orig: SoftBank swings to $7 billion loss after U.S. data center hit and Intel share decline
articles.title_zh: SoftBank swings to $7 billion loss after U.S. data center hit and Intel share decline
articles.content_orig:
SoftBank reported a fiscal second-quarter net loss of 1.12 trillion yen ($7 billion) on Tuesday, as losses tied to U.S. AI data center equipment procurement and Intel share declines weighed on earnings.
The Japanese investment giant also recorded a 597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) yen loss in the six months ending on Sept. 30 due to changes in procurement plans for power generation equipment for AI data center projects in the U.S.
SoftBank said it had made advance investments to secure power generation equipment for its AI data center projects in the U.S. amid concerns over potential shortages and long procurement lead times. Power is increasingly becoming a key constraint for the AI data center buildout as power grids become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.
Cumulative payments for power-generation equipment for U.S. AI data center projects, like the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Pike County, Ohio, totaled $9.48 billion as of the end of September.
"We made bridge investments in advance to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortage," a SoftBank executive said during the company's earnings call.
Here's how SoftBank fared in the fiscal second quarter:
Revenue rose 13.3% in the six months ended Sept. 30, supported by growth in telecommunications and AI computing businesses. The company said its SoftBank segment recorded higher sales across all businesses, while revenue at its AI computing segment increased.
The company's Vision Fund segment swung to a loss of 81.58 billion yen in the fiscal second quarter, compared with a profit of 2.38 trillion yen a year earlier. Vision Fund 1 recorded an investment loss of $20 million in the quarter, despite a $1.3 billion gain on ByteDance, as shares of publicly traded portfolio companies, including Coupang and Grab, declined.
The Vision Funds segment recorded investment gains of 85.45 billion yen, down sharply from 2.81 trillion yen in the year-earlier period. Vision Fund 2 posted investment gains of 89.26 billion yen, while Vision Fund 1 recorded a loss of 3.86 billion yen on its investments.
As of the end of September, SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI stood at $54.6 billion, with a fair value of $99.6 billion and a cumulative investment gain of $45 billion, according to the company.
SoftBank said a potential increase in OpenAI's valuation following a new funding round had not yet been reflected in its results, pending an official announcement. The updated valuation could be reflected in the fiscal third quarter, potentially boosting its net asset value and improving its loan-to-value ratio, the company said.
"ChatGPT has been continuously a weapon of OpenAI, especially for consumers," the SoftBank esecutive said during the company's earnings call, highlighting the chatbot's growing user base.
Shares of the Japanese investment giant closed 13.9% higher on Tuesday. The gains came as Asian technology stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, rose following an overnight rebound on Wall Street.
On its AI infrastructure investments, SoftBank highlighted a 20-year lease agreement with OpenAI for eight gigawatts of IT capacity at a data center project in Ohio.
Addressing concerns of water consumption at its planned data center in Texas, SoftBank said it was taking steps to reduce water use through a closed-loop, air-cooled system. The company also pointed to plans to hire and source locally.
Ahead of its earnings release, SoftBank Group announced on Monday plans with Grab and Malaysia's PETROS to commit a combined $1.85 billion in initial capital to develop AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with a long-term target of at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Filing Snafu Jolts Investors in Run-Up to Mega IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Filing Snafu Jolts Investors in Run-Up to Mega IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering could be a crucial test of investor confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, CNBC's Jim Cramer said on Monday.
"Without it, I don't see how the AI-related stocks can make a real recovery," the " Mad Money " host said, exactly two weeks after the Claude developer filed its S-1 IPO paperwork. Despite the recent sell-off in AI stocks, Anthropic is reportedly moving ahead with its IPO plans. The company is expected to meet with major investors this week and is targeting a trading debut as early as Thursday or Friday of next week, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter. "I don't think it's hyperbolic to say that this could be one of the most consequential IPOs in history."
Cramer explained that the billions of dollars being spent on AI chips and data centers ultimately depend on a handful of AI developers, including Anthropic, generating enough revenue to justify those investments.
"Anthropic is important because it is one of just a few companies at the end of the food chain for all of the AI data center investments that we've seen, so it is one of the few companies that, ultimately, needs to make money from all of this investment spending," Cramer said. "If it can't do that, or if it cannot convince enough investors that it will do so, then it's tough to justify all of the AI investments that are being made today."
Cramer pointed to SpaceX as an example of how interconnected the AI trade has become. Much of the Elon Musk rocket and AI company's recent revenue growth has come from renting computing capacity to customers, including Alphabet's Google and Anthropic. Google pays roughly $900 million a month for that capacity, while Anthropic's commitment has grown from an initial $1.25 billion monthly to more than $3 billion, according to its IPO prospectus.
Those contracts allow for SpaceX's massive purchases of Nvidia chips. "But if an Anthropic deal fails?" Cramer said. "Then Anthropic wouldn't have the cash to fulfill its contracts, and you'd have to take down estimates for both SpaceX and Nvidia, along with a whole host of other compute providers to Anthropic, and their suppliers." Not to mention, Alphabet, Amazon , and Nvidia have all invested in Anthropic, making their earnings sensitive to changes in the AI developer's valuation.
The wrinkle here is that investor appetite for an Anthropic IPO appears to be weakening. Anthropic's potential valuation has reportedly fallen from as much as $2 trillion earlier this fall to as low as $1 trillion following last week's technology sell-off on concerns that the Democratic wave in the midterm election will mean slower new data center construction.

articles.title_zh: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.
Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.
Both are innovators revered in the tech world.  However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.
In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.
Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.
I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.
It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.
An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.
He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.
"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."
He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.
However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.
Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.
The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.
He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.
Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".
He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".
At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.
More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.
Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.
Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.
It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

articles.title_orig: US demands a seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
articles.title_zh: US demands a seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
articles.content_orig:
ABU DHABI — European governments’ long-running and sometimes bad-tempered debate over who should represent them in Ukraine peace talks just became urgent.
Donald Trump’s envoys are pressing Russia to allow Europe to join the next round of negotiations aimed at resolving the Ukraine war, according to U.S. officials granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff will push the case for Europe to have a direct role in future talks as they mediate the first trilateral discussion with Russia and Ukraine since February in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the officials said.
European governments and EU institutions will likely not have long to decide who they want at the negotiating table on their behalf. Kushner and Witkoff want to step up the pace of the talks and for this week’s meeting to be the last without Europe’s full participation, the same officials said.
“We need Europe at the table,” one of the officials said. “So our proposal is to bring the Europeans into the discussion after this trilateral.”
The officials welcomed the fact that the leaders of Finland and Norway called Russia’s Vladimir Putin directly on Oct. 27 and said more outreach is necessary. “We need a lot more European discussions with Russia so that they could be hearing what we’re hearing and the message that they’re conveying to us they could be conveying to Russia directly.”
The question of who speaks for Europe — and whether Ukraine’s European allies should even be speaking to Putin at all — has been deeply divisive . EU leaders will discuss the topic at an informal summit in Dublin later this week.
Ever since Trump returned to the White House last year, EU officials and diplomats have been fretting about being left on the sidelines while the U.S. talks directly to Russia to negotiate an end to the war.
Senior European officials are due in Abu Dhabi for the meetings this week but, although Kushner and Witkoff are expected to consult them, they will not be involved in the main negotiations due to Russian objections. Those present include security advisers from the U.K., Germany, France, as well as officials from Italy, NATO, the European Commission and European Council.
The U.S. officials said Day 1 of the talks would focus on security guarantees for Ukraine and the potential reshaping of the security architecture of Europe. Day 2 would look at territorial issues — where the borders and boundaries should be drawn — and other questions.
European governments fear that Trump may be preparing to agree to longstanding demands from Putin to roll back NATO’s influence in the region. But the U.S. officials insisted that NATO would still be central to Europe’s collective defense, while refusing to back away from the need for a fundamental rethink of the continent’s relations with Russia.
“Obviously something’s not working,” the same official said. Europeans have “a lot of baggage” about redrawing the security architecture because Russia had proposed various changes in the past and previous arrangements had failed, the official said. “We have to build something new that works today.”
The officials said NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte had been heavily involved in the discussions with the U.S. administration and in sharing ideas for reforms.
On the most difficult question of all for Ukraine — the fate of Russian-occupied territory — both sides have shown “flexibility” in private, the officials said. The aim of this week’s talks is to keep up the momentum of recent weeks, rather than to deliver a final ceasefire, they added.
But the two main tracks in the talks — territory and future security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe — must run together and be resolved together, the U.S. side said.

articles.title_orig: Why COP31 may be the EU’s last great climate hurrah
articles.title_zh: Why COP31 may be the EU’s last great climate hurrah
articles.content_orig:
ANTALYA, Turkey—The stench of fossil fuels has become a hallmark of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, starting with the airplanes and buses carrying delegates to the conferences.
Two annual meetings have been held in Poland, where coal remains king. Eye-searing petrochemical smog marred the skies over Dubai at COP28. In Baku, Azerbaijan, most buildings are coated with gray grime from refinery pollution, and last year at the “Nature COP” in Belém, Brazil, hundreds of diesel generators ran day and night outside the conference halls in a futile effort to cool the heavy tropical air.
The latest iteration of the negotiations, COP31, opened Monday here with diesel fumes in the city’s busy streets providing another reminder that the world remains deeply dependent on the fossil fuels driving the climate crisis even after three decades of climate negotiations.
The backdrop to this year’s conference is bleak. Scientists report that the average global temperature has reached a record high of more than 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius) above the preindustrial baseline in the last few days. Several dozen glaciers have disappeared since last year’s talks. Rising seas are flooding coastal cities. And carbon dioxide emissions in 2026 are on track to reach another record high.
The climate crisis didn’t reach this point overnight, said Marc Hudson , an unaffiliated climate researcher in the United Kingdom. It is the culmination of decades of missed opportunities, political compromises and broken promises. Understanding how it happened requires revisiting a surreal and occasionally absurd history, he said.
A convenient starting point is 1957, when scientists from around the world shared research and met repeatedly to study Earth as a system, rather than individual components, as part of the International Geophysical Year . It was also when American scientist Charles Keeling began developing a system to measure the rise of CO2 in the global atmosphere, and when a landmark research paper challenged the assumption that the oceans could absorb CO2 emissions from fossil fuel burning.
It’s clear from the scientific record, Hudson said, that researchers understood the looming problem nearly 70 years ago.
But the issue did not appear on political radar screens until 1985, when scientists at an international climate conference in Austria warned that rising CO2 levels could produce climate warming greater than any in human history, with significant consequences for agriculture, ecosystems and people.
The researchers urged governments to start considering policy responses. A few years later, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was born. In 1990, the panel issued its first major climate assessment , spurring the United Nations to action.
Representatives from more than 140 countries spent 15 months negotiating the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change . At that point, about 10 industrialized countries were responsible for about 80 percent of all historic CO2 emissions. There was broad agreement that those nations should take the lead in reducing climate-altering pollution and that any treaty should not deny poorer countries the chance to develop.
That disagreement remains one of the defining features of climate diplomacy, and the United States has been central to that debate since the beginning, Hudson said. George H.W. Bush, a former fossil-fuel industry executive, was president, and he was “even more sympathetic than the Democrats to big auto, big oil,” Hudson said. The Bush administration feared that the international community would mobilize against carbon dioxide emissions in much the same way it had against ozone depletion just a few years earlier.
France and a few other European countries pushed for a treaty that would obligate rich, industrialized countries to set timetables for emission cuts, but it was “very important for the Americans and the Saudis and the Gulf oil and gas exporters that whatever deal emerged from an international negotiating process was as weak as possible,” Hudson said. Bush threatened to boycott the 1992 Rio Earth Summit if a treaty included binding language on emissions cuts.
The French and other proponents of emissions-reduction targets had to choose between pressing ahead with a strong treaty that the U.S. wouldn’t sign or watering down the agreement to secure American support.
“This was straightforward, naked power politics,” Hudson said. “The Americans and the Saudis wanted to make sure that they could keep on selling and using fossil fuels for as long as they wanted, and they didn’t want to have to negotiate on actual emissions reductions.”
In the final weeks of negotiations for the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change agreement, references to binding cuts were removed from the draft and the U.S. became an early signatory because it was “no longer worried about what was becoming a toothless agreement,” and setting the stage for the first Conference of the Parties, COP1, in Berlin, Hudson said.
The climate framework was vague, but it included an agreement to try to stabilize emissions at 1990 levels. Most people involved in the talks hoped a more detailed agreement with timetables and national plans would soon follow, said Joanna Depledge , a climate diplomacy researcher at the University of Cambridge.
Most probably never would have believed that emissions would still be increasing 30 years later, she added.
The early international steps toward tackling global warming came after the end of the Cold War, as former adversaries sought to cooperate, she said.

But then, as now, she added, the U.S. was reluctant to accept an agreement that would put the onus on developed countries to reduce emissions first and was reluctant to assume any financial obligations toward developing countries. This worldview has continued shaping the climate talks for 30 years.
At COP1 in Berlin in 1995, delegates acknowledged that the U.N.’s climate framework alone would not solve the emerging global warming problem, so they agreed to keep meeting to reach a follow-up deal with quantifiable emission-reduction targets for industrialized countries. Since then, the 198 countries party to the climate framework have met 29 more times to try and implement those basic ideas.
Just two years later, the Kyoto Protocol, with obligatory emissions reductions for industrialized countries, was adopted at COP3. But just before the conference, the U.S. Senate passed the Byrd-Hagel Resolution by a vote of 95–0, declaring that it would not ratify an agreement on emissions cuts that did not require similar commitments from developing countries, or that would harm the U.S. economy.
President Bill Clinton signed the agreement in 1998, which may have been a high-water mark for U.S. engagement in the process, at least until the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, Depledge said. But Clinton never sent it to the Senate.
In 2001, his successor, President George W. Bush, said the U.S. would not ratify the Kyoto Protocol, taking momentum away from the global push to curb global warming.

articles.content_orig:

The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped about 1,100 points on Monday, and Warren Buffett’s rule for exactly this moment is 18 years old: “So if you wait for the robins, spring will be over.” He wrote it in The New York Times on Oct. 17, 2008, a month after Lehman Brothers failed, in a piece titled “Buy American. I Am.” The sentence before it said what he meant: “What is likely, however, is that the market will move higher, perhaps substantially so, well before either sentiment or the economy turns up.”
Monday fit the rule. The Dow rose more than 2% to roughly 52,400. The S&P 500 index fund rose 2.4%, its biggest gain since April 8, and the Nasdaq-100 fund rose 3.5%. That came three trading days after the S&P 500 fund’s 4.4% drop on Thursday, its worst day since April 2025, and one trading day after stocks closed their worst week since the tariff week of April 2025. The worries that drove last week’s selling had not been settled over the weekend. The main change on Monday was a drop in oil prices.
Monday’s 1,100 points are a warning about the cost of waiting for the all-clear: the rebound came while the worries that caused the selling were still there, which is what Buffett’s rule says to expect. They are also one day, and one day says nothing about whether last Thursday was the low.
Take a retired couple, 66 and 63, with $1.8 million: $1,250,000 in a rollover IRA, $400,000 in a brokerage account and $150,000 in a Roth. They hold 65% in an S&P 500 index fund, $1,170,000 at Friday’s close, and $630,000 in bonds and a money market fund. Social Security pays them $4,800 a month, $57,600 a year, and they spend $118,000, so they draw $60,400 a year from the portfolio, 3.4% of it. On Friday afternoon, after a week of headlines, he typed an order to move $600,000 of the IRA’s index fund to cash, the money market fund, until things settled down. He did not send it. If you typed something like it, here is what the order would have cost by Monday’s close, what Buffett’s rule cost the people who followed it in 2008 before it paid them, and the one number that should decide this for you instead of the Dow.
Their stock sleeve was worth $1,239,695 at the S&P 500’s Oct. 6 record. Thursday took $53,799 out of it in one session. It closed Friday at $1,170,000 and Monday at $1,197,607, a gain of $27,607 in a day, and it is still $42,087 under the record.
The $600,000 that was almost in the money market fund would have missed $14,158 of Monday’s gain. That is one day. The larger cost is the one Buffett’s sentence describes. If you sell until it settles down, you need a signal that it has settled, and the usual one is the index back at its record. The S&P 500 fund’s record is 6.0% above Friday’s close, so $600,000 that waits for that signal buys back $566,268 worth of Friday’s shares, $33,732 less, and only if the record is the first sign of calm. In exchange, the money market fund would pay you about 4.17%, the 3-month Treasury bill rate: $25,020 a year, or $2,085 a month.
Buffett was careful to say what the rule does not do. “Let me be clear on one point: I can’t predict the short-term movements of the stock market,” he wrote, and he was right to be careful. He published on Oct. 17, 2008, with the S&P 500 fund at $93.21. It kept falling for five months, to $68.11 on March 9, 2009, a loss of 26.9% after his piece ran. If you had bought that week because of it, you were down by more than a quarter by spring.
Then the robins came late, exactly as he said. The recession ended in June 2009, but the National Bureau of Economic Research did not announce that until Sept. 20, 2010, and by that day the fund had risen 67.7% from its low. A year after the piece ran, the fund was up 17.8% from where he published. Five years after, 85.8%. Today it is 8.07 times the price on the day it ran, price only, with dividends excluded: $100,000 held through all of it is $807,467. The same $100,000 rolled in 3-month Treasury bills since that day is $129,634. His other line in the piece was about that choice: “Today people who hold cash equivalents feel comfortable. They shouldn’t.”
The reason the rule works is in the calendar of the S&P 500 fund’s daily closes since 2000. Of its 20 best days in that span, 12 came within 10 trading days of one of its 20 worst days. The two biggest, Oct. 13, 2008 (up 14.5%) and Oct. 28, 2008 (up 11.7%), landed in the middle of the worst stretch of the crisis. The third biggest, April 9, 2025 (up 10.5%), came three trading days after the tariff drop that still marks the last week worse than the one just ended.
That clustering is what a sell-and-wait order buys you. $100,000 put in the fund on Jan. 3, 2000, and left alone was worth $517,501 on Monday, 6.31% a year, price only. If you missed the 10 best days, you have $224,552, 3.06% a year. If you missed the 20 best, you have $131,516, 1.03% a year, less than the $169,619 that 3-month Treasury bills returned over the same stretch. Those 20 days are fewer than one a year, and most of them fell in the weeks when you would most have wanted to be out.
The rule says the recovery arrives before the all-clear. It does not say when, and it does not say Monday was the start of it. In 2008 the fund fell another 26.9% after Buffett wrote, and the 1,100 points the Dow gained on Monday leave the S&P 500 fund 3.4% below its record and the Nasdaq-100 fund 10.6% below its own. If you draw $60,400 a year, you cannot wait five years for the robins with money you need next year, and Buffett was writing about his personal account, which he said had held nothing but Treasury bonds until then.
That is why the decision for this couple belongs to a different number than the Dow. Their $630,000 outside stocks covers 10.4 years of draws at $60,400 a year. The 2007 to 2009 fall took the S&P 500 fund 5.4 years to repair, from its October 2007 peak to the first close above it in March 2013, and the 2000 to 2002 fall took 7.2 years. A reserve that covers a decade means no stock has to be sold in a bad year, which is the only thing the Friday order was trying to buy, at a cost of $14,158 on its first day. If your real worry is the mix, that 65% in stocks is more than you can sleep with at 66, change it once, inside the IRA where it costs you nothing in tax, and pick the day from your plan, which does not care what the Dow did on Monday.
The Dow rose about 1,100 points on Monday, the S&P 500 fund had its biggest day since April 8, and the worries that caused last week’s selling were still there when it happened. That is the moment Buffett’s 2008 rule describes: the market moves first, the news catches up later, and the people who wait for the robins miss spring. His rule cost its followers 26.9% in the five months after he wrote it and paid them 85.8% within five years. For a couple with $1.8 million, the $600,000 order that was never sent would have missed $14,158 on Monday and $33,732 of shares if they waited for the record to buy back. The number that should settle it for you is 10.4 years, the draws their bonds and cash already cover, and that number was the same on Thursday night as it is tonight.

articles.title_orig: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
articles.title_zh: US-Iran war: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz . However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

articles.title_orig: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.title_zh: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.content_orig:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.
CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.
As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title_orig: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.title_zh: After meeting Qatar PM, Trump calls Iran war ‘effectively over’ militarily
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has signalled that he considers the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively” at an end, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister in Washington, DC.
In a surprise briefing on Monday, Trump reiterated his position that the US had destroyed Iran’s military. But his remarks suggested he faces pressure from allies in the Middle East to bring hostilities to a close.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” he said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
His comments followed a closed-door meeting with US Vice President JD Vance and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, who hailed the progress in a post on social media.
“We discussed the situation in the region and ways to progress the US-Iran talks,” the prime minister said. “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.”
Still, Trump acknowledged the “status quo” would involve continuing the US naval blockade against Iranian ports, as well as the newly announced Task Force Iron Gate, which seeks to cut off trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.
“Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others would prefer the status quo, that we remain as is,” he said. “In other words, a continuation of the greatest naval blockade in the history of our country. Probably in the history of the world.”
Trump also indicated in his briefing that the US was willing to resume fighting, should the need arise.
“Taking military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes,” he said.
“Israel and the entire Middle East are protected from Iranian danger and threats, and we’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.”
Iranian officials, meanwhile, dismissed Trump’s latest remarks as a distraction.
“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler,” Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote in a post on social media.
“FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks.”
Separately, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the country’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had called for an end to the situation, which he described as “neither war nor peace”.
Pezeshkian added that Iran was open to further negotiations but would not be coerced, according to Iranian media. “We will not surrender to force and bullying,” he said.
Since the war on Iran began on February 28, the conflict has spilled into surrounding countries and roiled international trade.
Almost as soon as the US and Israel began their attacks, Iran moved to shut down the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil, gas and fertiliser, among other goods.
Iran also responded to US and Israeli strikes with missile and drone fire on its neighbours in the Gulf, including Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE, with many of the attacks targeting US military installations.
Other, related conflicts have since emerged. Saudi Arabia has renewed its fight against the Iran-backed Houthis, and Israel began its occupation of southern Lebanon, as well as deadly air strikes.
In the nearly nine months since the war began, the US offensive against Iran has grown sporadic, with intermittent exchanges of fire.
In recent days, for instance, the Trump administration announced “minor strikes” against Iran’s Qeshm Island.
It also offered a $20m reward for “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel”.
After the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, Trump had claimed that Iran’s uranium enrichment programme had been obliterated. But he has since made curtailing Iran’s nuclear programme a central premise for the ongoing war.
Iran has long denied seeking a nuclear weapon, maintaining its uranium enrichment programme is for the purposes of civilian energy generation.
Officials in Iran, meanwhile, have pushed for the US to accept seven conditions in order to end the war.
They include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, recognising a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz worked out with Oman, and ending the war on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.
Qatar has served as one of several key mediators in the conflict. Sheikh Mohammed, the prime minister, also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.
In Monday’s closed-door meeting, he reportedly presented Trump with a two-day proposal from Iran to end the war.
Afterwards, reporters asked Trump in the briefing room, “Why not just declare an end to the conflict and be done with it?”
Trump replied by framing the continued US blockade as a question of regional security. He also called for a “long-term solution”, rather than a short-term one.
“We have some great allies there, and we have to make sure they’re not hurt, and they would be hurt,” he said.
“They are right now a lot safer than they were six months ago because Iran’s been very much decapitated. But they’re still the bully of the Middle East a little bit.”

This past week's stock market meltdown could hardly have come at a more critical moment for Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ). The sell-off cast a shadow over the frontier artificial intelligence developer's expected pre-Thanksgiving public debut, raising questions about its potential valuation and ability to sustain the next phase of AI growth.
"The only thing that matters the rest of this year is the Anthropic IPO," said Neostellar principal Willy Lee on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. Lee said investors want to know whether Anthropic can sustain long-term growth and secure a meaningful share of the AI market.
"Those are the two questions that every investor is asking within their investment committee every single day before the IPO," said Lee.
Anthropic recently revealed revenue grew $1,206% to $33.2 billion through the first nine months of the year. The company also noted a staggering aggregate committed spend of $895.4 billion , which it says is primarily related to compute and infrastructure.
But the AI growth story was put to the test this past week as investors weighed a Democratic congressional win against the impact of the AI data center build-out. On Thursday, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) suffered its worst daily decline since April 2025, with chip stocks leading the declines.
The market turmoil prompted prospective buyers to discuss lowering Anthropic's valuation to a range of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, with some considering as low as $1.1 trillion, according to Bloomberg. That's far below estimates as high as $2 trillion projected in early October.
Amid increasingly jittery sentiment toward AI stocks, Anthropic faces a difficult decision, particularly if the unwinding of the AI trade continues.
"It would be difficult to go public," Anna Rathbun, founder and CEO of Grenadilla Advisory, told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
If Anthropic decides to delay its IPO, investors could interpret the move as a bearish signal for the AI trade, said Kevin Mahn, chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh.
"If they don't delay, and their IPO fails, or comes in below expectations, that could be perceived as bearish to certain investors," said Mahn. "Damned if you do, damned if you don't."
Investors will also be looking for clues about the health of the AI trade on Nov. 17, when Nvidia ( NVDA ) reports earnings. With hyperscalers Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Meta ( META ) having already reported, along with foundry Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) and chip equipment maker ASML ( ASML ), expectations are high that Nvidia will once again beat earnings estimates and raise its guidance.
"We got so much confirmation already," said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum. "I give it a 1% chance that they miss."

articles.title_zh: SoftBank Group shares surge 13% as Asian tech stocks track Wall Street rebound
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week's bruising sell-off.
Japan's technology investment giant SoftBank Group rose 13.88%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest gained 4.63%.
Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron rose over 6.05%, while Lasertec and Disco advanced 7.73% and 6.81%, respectively.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 6.69%, while Samsung Electronics rose 4.74%. Samsung SDI climbed 9.88%. Taiwan's TSMC added 2.24%.
China's tech-heavy ChiNext Price Index rose 1.46%.
The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.
The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure.
"This is not to suggest that the tech sell-off is done and dusted. While there is some evidence that investors are taking advantage of last week's plunge to increase their exposure to chip and other AI-adjacent stocks, there's a danger that it may be a little bit premature to load up and 'buy the dip,'" said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.
Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.

Federal regulators have launched a preliminary evaluation into more than 1.2 million Ford vehicles after side airbags deployed during crashes reportedly left multiple occupants with severe burns requiring medical treatment.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened the probe last Friday.
The notice affects 2021-2026 model Ford Explorer vehicles , including Explorer Police Interceptors used by law enforcement.
Side airbag deployments reportedly caused second and third-degree burns to front-seat occupants, regulators said.
